title: How the JavaScript Prototype Chain Works
summary: Understand JavaScript prototype chain lookup, the difference between prototype and [[Prototype]], how inherited properties are shadowed, and how to inspect object links safely.
body_markdown:
When you read a property, JavaScript checks the object’s own properties first, then follows its internal` \[\[Prototype\]\]` link to the next object, and repeats until it either finds the property or reaches` null` , in which case the read returns` undefined` .


That rule is simple, but it gets harder to follow once you see` prototype` ,` __proto__` and` \[\[Prototype\]\]` next to each other in a DevTools panel or an interview question. Firefox even labels the link` <prototype>` when you expand an object in the console.


This article covers only how a property lookup walks the chain: which object answers a read, where writes land, and which APIs to use to inspect a prototype. For constructor functions, classes and` Object.create` inheritance patterns, see[A Beginner’s Guide to OOP in JavaScript](https://blog.openreplay.com/a-beginners-guide-to-oop-in-javascript/) and[Inheritance in JavaScript Object-Oriented Programming](https://blog.openreplay.com/inheritance-in-javascript-object-oriented-programming/) .


## Key Takeaways


- A property read checks own properties, then each` \[\[Prototype\]\]` in turn, and returns` undefined` once the chain ends at` null` .
- A function’s` prototype` property becomes the` \[\[Prototype\]\]` of instances created with` new` . It is not the function’s own prototype.
- ` __proto__` is a deprecated accessor inherited from` Object.prototype` . Use` Object.getPrototypeOf()` and` Object.setPrototypeOf()` instead.
- Assigning to an inherited property usually creates an own property that shadows the inherited one and leaves the prototype unchanged.
- ` Object.create(null)` produces an object with no chain, which makes it a safe dictionary for arbitrary string keys.


## What Is the JavaScript Prototype Chain Lookup Rule?


The JavaScript prototype chain is the sequence of objects, linked through` \[\[Prototype\]\]` , that a property read walks until it finds a match or reaches` null` . Every ordinary object has an internal` \[\[Prototype\]\]` slot that points to another object or to` null` . The specification’s[OrdinaryGet algorithm](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-ordinaryget) defines how a read works. It looks for an own property, and if there isn’t one, it repeats the lookup on the prototype. For most objects, the chain ends at` Object.prototype` , whose prototype is` null` .


```text
const   animal   =   {   eats  :   true   };
const   rabbit   =   Object  .  create  (  animal  );
rabbit  .  jumps   =   true  ;


console  .  log  (  rabbit  .  jumps  );     // true      (own property)
console  .  log  (  rabbit  .  eats  );      // true      (found on animal)
console  .  log  (  rabbit  .  toString   ===   Object  .  prototype  .  toString  );   // true
console  .  log  (  rabbit  .  flies  );     // undefined (not found anywhere)
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  Object  .  prototype  ));   // null
// rabbit -> animal -> Object.prototype -> null
```


A missing property is not an error when you read it. *Calling*` rabbit.flies()` is what throws a` TypeError` , because the call is made on` undefined` . MDN’s[Inheritance and the prototype chain](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Inheritance_and_the_prototype_chain) guide covers the same model in more depth.


## What Is the Difference Between a Function’s prototype and an Object’s \[\[Prototype\]\]?


A function’s` prototype` property is the object that becomes the` \[\[Prototype\]\]` of instances created with` new` . It is not the function’s own prototype, which is` Function.prototype` . To read the real link on any object, use[Object.getPrototypeOf()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/getPrototypeOf) .


```text
class   Greeter   {   hello  () {   return   '  hi  '  ; } }
const   g   =   new   Greeter  ();


console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  g  )   ===   Greeter  .  prototype  );          // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  Greeter  )   ===   Function  .  prototype  );   // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  Greeter  )   ===   Greeter  .  prototype  );    // false


const   arrow   =   ()   =>   {};
console  .  log  (  arrow  .  prototype  );                     // undefined
console  .  log  (  Greeter  .  prototype  .  hello  .  prototype  );   // undefined
```


Arrow functions and plain class methods have no` prototype` property at all, so reading` .prototype` on them returns` undefined` .

## What Is **proto** ?


` __proto__` is an accessor property defined on` Object.prototype` . It is not stored on each object, so an object that doesn’t inherit from` Object.prototype` doesn’t have it. MDN marks[Object.prototype.__proto__](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/proto) as Deprecated and explains that it is in the standard only so older websites keep working. MDN recommends` Object.getPrototypeOf()` and[Object.setPrototypeOf()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/setPrototypeOf) instead.


```text
const   proto   =   {   greet  ()   {   return   '  hello  '  ;   }   };
const   obj   =   Object  .  create  (  proto  );


console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  obj  )   ===   proto  );            // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  hasOwn  (  obj  ,   '  __proto__  '  ));                 // false
console  .  log  (  Object  .  hasOwn  (  Object  .  prototype  ,   '  __proto__  '  ));    // true


const   bare   =   Object  .  create  (  null  );
console  .  log  (  bare  .  __proto__  );                                  // undefined


const   lit   =   {   __proto__  :   proto   };
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  lit  )   ===   proto  );            // true
```


The` { __proto__: value }` key in an[object literal](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Object_initializer) is standard syntax and separate from the accessor. It is not deprecated. Only the colon form sets the prototype. A computed` \["__proto__"\]` key creates an ordinary own property.


Even with the proper API, try not to change a prototype after an object is created. MDN warns that doing so is “currently a very slow operation in every browser and JavaScript engine.” Set the prototype when you create the object instead.


## Shadowing: Own Properties Hide Inherited Ones


Lookup stops at the first match, so an own property hides any property with the same name further up the chain. Assignment works the same way. Unless an inherited setter or a non-writable inherited property gets in the way, the specification’s[OrdinarySet](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-ordinaryset) creates or updates an own property on the target object. The inherited property is shadowed, not changed.


```text
const   defaults   =   {   theme  :   '  light  '   };
const   settings   =   Object  .  create  (  defaults  );


console  .  log  (  settings  .  theme  );                      // 'light' (inherited)
settings  .  theme   =   '  dark  '  ;                          // creates an own property
console  .  log  (  defaults  .  theme  );                      // 'light' (prototype untouched)
console  .  log  (  Object  .  hasOwn  (  settings  ,   '  theme  '  ));    // true


delete   settings  .  theme  ;
console  .  log  (  settings  .  theme  );                      // 'light' (inherited again)
// settings -> defaults -> Object.prototype -> null
```


[Object.hasOwn()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/hasOwn) tells you which layer answered a read. MDN recommends it in place of` hasOwnProperty()` .


## How Do Array.prototype Methods Reach Every Array?


Every array created with an array literal has` Array.prototype` as its` \[\[Prototype\]\]` . That is why` map` ,` filter` and` push` work on every array without being copied onto it. Built-ins rely on shadowing too:[Array.prototype.toString](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/toString) hides` Object.prototype.toString` .


```text
const   nums   =   [  1  ,   2  ,   3  ];


console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  nums  )   ===   Array  .  prototype  );               // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  hasOwn  (  nums  ,   '  map  '  ));                                    // false
console  .  log  (  nums  .  map   ===   Array  .  prototype  .  map  );                              // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  Array  .  prototype  )   ===   Object  .  prototype  );   // true


console  .  log  (  nums  .  toString  ());                         // '1,2,3'
console  .  log  (  Object  .  prototype  .  toString  .  call  (  nums  ));    // '[object Array]'
// nums -> Array.prototype -> Object.prototype -> null
```


## Object.create(null) for Objects With No Chain


[Object.create(null)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/create) creates an object whose` \[\[Prototype\]\]` is` null` . It inherits nothing: no` toString` , no` hasOwnProperty` , no` __proto__` accessor. A null-prototype object is therefore a safe container for keys that come from user input. With a plain` {}` , inherited names such as` constructor` already return a value before you store anything.


```text
const   words   =   [  '  a  '  ,   '  constructor  '  ,   '  a  '  ];


const   plain   =   {};
for (  const   w   of   words  )   plain  [  w  ]   =   (  plain  [  w  ]   ??   0  )   +   1  ;
console  .  log  (  plain  .  constructor  );   // a string like "function Object() { [native code] }1"


const   counts   =   Object  .  create  (  null  );
for (  const   w   of   words  )   counts  [  w  ]   =   (  counts  [  w  ]   ??   0  )   +   1  ;
console  .  log  (  counts  .  constructor  );     // 1
console  .  log  (  counts  .  a  );               // 2
console  .  log  (  '  toString  '   in   counts  );   // false
// counts -> null
```


A[null-prototype object](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object#null-prototype_objects) has no inherited methods, so call` Object.hasOwn(counts, key)` rather than` counts.hasOwnProperty(key)` . Interpolating it into a template literal throws a` TypeError` because there is no` toString` to convert it to a string. When keys aren’t strings, use a[Map](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map) .


## Do Classes Use the Same Prototype Chain?


Yes. Class syntax does not add a new inheritance model. Methods declared in a class body live on` ClassName.prototype` , and instances reach them through the same` \[\[Prototype\]\]` lookup as any other object.[extends](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Classes/extends) links one class’s` prototype` object to the parent’s.


```text
class   Animal   {   speak  () {   return   '  sound  '  ; } }
class   Dog   extends   Animal   {   bark  () {   return   '  woof  '  ; } }
const   d   =   new   Dog  ();


console  .  log  (  typeof   Dog  );                                                  // 'function'
console  .  log  (  Object  .  hasOwn  (  d  ,   '  speak  '  ));                                   // false
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  d  )   ===   Dog  .  prototype  );                  // true
console  .  log  (  Object  .  getPrototypeOf  (  Dog  .  prototype  )   ===   Animal  .  prototype  );   // true
console  .  log  (  d  .  speak  ());                                                   // 'sound'
// d -> Dog.prototype -> Animal.prototype -> Object.prototype -> null
```


## Conclusion


Every property read follows the same path. JavaScript checks the object itself, then each` \[\[Prototype\]\]` in turn until it finds the property or reaches` null` . Writes stay on the object you assign to. Next time a value looks like it came from nowhere, run` Object.hasOwn()` on the object, then call` Object.getPrototypeOf()` on each link and write out the chain until you find the object that actually holds the property.


## FAQs


What is the difference between the in operator and Object.hasOwn()?


The in operator checks the whole prototype chain, so 'toString' in {} returns true because toString is inherited from Object.prototype. Object.hasOwn(obj, key) checks only the object's own properties and returns false for anything inherited. Use in when an inherited property should count, and Object.hasOwn() when you need to know whether the object itself holds the key.


How does instanceof use the prototype chain?


By default, obj instanceof C returns true if C.prototype appears anywhere in the prototype chain of obj. It does not prove that C created the object, because any object whose chain includes C.prototype passes. A class can replace this check by defining a static Symbol.hasInstance method. Primitive values on the left side always return false with the default check.


Do for...in loops and Object.keys() include inherited properties?


A for...in loop visits enumerable string-keyed properties on the object and on every object up its prototype chain. Object.keys(), Object.entries() and object spread include only the object's own enumerable properties. Methods on built-in prototypes such as Object.prototype and Array.prototype are non-enumerable, so they do not show up in for...in. Enumerable properties on your own prototype objects do.


Can a JavaScript prototype chain contain a cycle?


Not with ordinary objects. Object.setPrototypeOf() throws a TypeError if the new prototype would create a cycle, for example setting a's prototype to b when b already inherits from a. Assigning through the __proto__ setter throws the same error. Because cycles are rejected, a chain of ordinary objects is always finite and ends at null, so a property lookup always stops.
